snippet: HB467 prevents an abortion clinic from being licensed after May 2, 2023, and from operating on or after January 1, 2024, or when their license expires. The measure passed 22 to 6 on March 2, 2023. Senators Voting YES (22): J. Stuart Adams, Jacob L. Anderegg, Curtis S. Bramble, Gregg D. Buxton, Kirk A. Cullimore, Lincoln Fillmore, Keith Grover, Wayne A. Harper, David P. Hinkins, Don L. Ipson, John D. Johnson, Michael S. Kennedy, Daniel McCay, Michael K. McKell, Ann Millner, Derrin R. Owens, Scott D. Sandall, Jerry W. Stevenson, Evan J. Vickers, Todd D. Weiler, Chris H. Wilson, Ronald M. Winterton

The Legislature on Thursday approved a bill aimed at further limiting abortions in the state by banning elective abortion clinics after May 2. The measure, HB467, prohibits the new licensing of abortion clinics starting May 3, and forces any clinic to stop providing abortions when their existing license expires.

The 22 senators voting in favor included Stevenson along with Adams, Balderree, Brammer, Cullimore, Escamilla, Fillmore, Grover, Harper, Hinkins, Ipson, Johnson, McCay, McKell, Millner, Musselman, Owens, Sandall, Stratton, Weiler, Wilson, and Winterton. The 7 voting against included Blouin, Buss, Kwan, Pitcher, Plumb, Riebe, and Vickers.

A proposal allowing health care providers in the state to refuse treatment based on their deeply held beliefs — including religion or conscience — received final passage from the Utah Legislature. SB174, sponsored by Sen. Keven Stratton, R-Orem, now heads to Gov. Spencer Cox's desk.

The Senate voted 20-8 to pass SB16 on its final vote on January 27, 2023. Republicans voting NO: Sen. David Hinkins, R-Ferron, and Sen. Todd Weiler, R-Woods Cross, joined Democrats in voting against the bill. SB16 would ban transgender surgeries for Utah children and teens and place an indefinite moratorium on puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones for minors.
SB16 Ban on Sex Mutilation Against Minors (2023): YES — Banned transgender medical treatments for minors. Jerry W. Stevenson voted YES on SB16.

HB300 would require Utah voters to write the last four digits of their government-issued identification card on their ballot's return envelope. The bill would require voters to request a mail-in ballot every eight years starting in 2029.
HB300 Election Integrity (3/6/2025): YES — Required in-person ballot return with ID. Jerry W. Stevenson voted YES on HB300.

Just after the Utah Senate education committee voted 7-2 to advance House Bill 215, the Utah Fits All bill that would let students use public funds for private education, all nine members of the education committee represent part of the Wasatch Front. The seven senators voting for the bill, all Republicans, were Stuart Adams, Lincoln Fillmore, Keith Grover, John Johnson McKell, Ann Millner and Jerry Stevenson. The two votes against were by Kathleen Riebe, a Cottonwood Heights Democrat, and David Hinkins.

The Senate voted 20-8 Thursday to approve the bill, which now heads to the desk of Gov. Spencer Cox. The legislation provides $8,000 scholarships to qualifying families for private schools and other private education options. The Utah Fits All Scholarship program can be used for education expenses like curriculum, textbooks, education, software, tutoring services, micro-school teacher salaries and private school tuition.

On April 24, MIDA's board, chaired by Adams, approved a 40,000-acre hyperscale data center campus and natural gas power plant in northern Utah backed by Kevin O'Leary. The board gave unanimous approval of Resolution 2026-08, approving and authorizing the execution of a development agreement. Stevenson sat on the MIDA board and voted unanimously to approve the first project ever activated under his own law — without disclosing any conflict and without recusing himself. Stevenson personally sponsored SB232 (Chapter 463, 2022) — the bill that rewrote Utah Code § 63H-1-401, eliminated the contiguity requirement for private land in MIDA project areas, and made county consent irrevocable.

Sen. Jerry Stevenson (R-Layton) is a voting board member of MIDA, having served since 2008. On Friday, April 24, the MIDA board green-lit a multibillion-dollar hyperscale data center project in Box Elder County, creating a new project area called Stratos that encompasses military Utah Test and Training Range land and collecting an estimated $49 million a year in property taxes from the project once it's fully built.

HB165 Illegal Immigration (2024): YES — Established requirements for federal officers releasing aliens in Utah. SB217 CHIP Benefits for Illegal Aliens (2023): NO. Jerry W. Stevenson voted YES on HB165 and NO on SB217.

Jerry Stevenson cast an opposing vote on SB262, an employment and housing anti-discrimination bill in a Senate committee hearing in 2013. The bill would prohibit discrimination at work or in housing on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, and would offer statewide protections.

In March 2020, the state legislature passed Senate Bill 200 (SB 200), which altered the state statute enacted by Proposition 4. SB 200 also repealed provisions that barred the commission and legislators from using partisan political data, such as partisan election results and voting records, when drafting maps, and from drawing districts that purposefully or unduly favored or disfavored any incumbent, candidate, or political party. The state Senate passed SB 200 by a vote of 25-0.

Lawmakers advance plan to cut Utah income taxes for sixth straight year. A bill to drop Utah's income tax rate from 4.5% to 4.45% — with a price tag of about $101 million in ongoing money — has already cleared the Utah Senate. Utah's Legislative session has produced income tax cuts for six consecutive years.

SB248 Expanding State-funded Childcare (2/25/2026): YES — would create a new program for employer-sponsored, state-assisted childcare facilities. HB100 Free School Meals (3/6/2025): YES — Expands access to free school meals extending no-cost lunch. Jerry W. Stevenson voted YES on both SB248 and HB100.

HB452 Carbon-capture Rules (2/29/2024): NO — Reforms and expands the regulation of carbon capture and storage. Jerry W. Stevenson voted NO on HB452, which set up a regulatory mechanism for inspection and long-term monitoring of carbon dioxide injection wells.
